title: Scaling AI-driven chip design with open agent factories
abstract: As AI systems become more capable, researchers are increasingly asking a practical question: Can AI do more than help write code for computing systems? Specifically, can it actively participate in the design of complex computing systems and rapidly translate algorithms into silicon? New work in AI-driven chip design suggests the answer is yes. But a promising algorithm is only the beginning of a hardware design. Turning it into an efficient chip requires exploring how to organize computation, move data, and use limited hardware resources. Each choice opens up alternatives. Each alternative takes engineering effort to implement and evaluate. AI agents can expand that exploration. Working together, they can propose architectural changes, write implementations, check correctness, and use synthesis results to decide what to try next. The obstacle is cost: the LLM tokenomics for hardware design and the cost-efficiency of design space exploration. A single search campaign can consume hundreds of millions of tokens, and applying the approach across many components and design revisions could require hundreds of such campaigns. A new demonstration from IBM Research shows how open frontier models and efficient distributed inference can change the calculation. Using an agent factory to optimize hardware for quantum error correction, researchers achieved a 52-times speedup over the baseline design in high-level synthesis estimates for approximately $26 in inference cost. Under the same search budget, a proprietary frontier model configuration cost 11.5 times more than a configuration using open frontier models throughout — $299 versus $26, respectively. The proprietary configuration achieved higher speedup (204x), but the open-model configuration established a different result: Substantial hardware optimization can be achieved with a much smaller inference budget, along with the smallest area design. That cost advantage creates an opportunity to apply automated exploration more widely, and to reinvest the savings in finding better designs. The results also suggest that the practical value of AI-assisted chip design depends on more than the best design an agent can produce. It also depends on how much verified exploration an organization can afford. Model capability, the assignment of agent roles, and the infrastructure serving those models all shape the hardware improvements that are attainable within a real engineering budget. By combining open frontier models with llm-d’s low-cost distributed inference , IBM has demonstrated that AI agent factories can move beyond coding assistance and become active participants in hardware design, and they can do it affordably. From generating code to exploring architectures Hardware design remains one of the most expertise-intensive activities in computing. High Level Synthesis (HLS) raises the level of abstraction from register-transfer level (RTL), used in hardware design languages, to C or C++, but engineers must still make countless decisions about loop structure, parallelism, memory organization, dataflow, and synthesis directives. Those choices interact in complex ways. For example, performing more calculations simultaneously helps only if the memory system can supply their inputs. A design that runs faster may also require more hardware resources. Finding a useful balance requires repeated experiments, and the design space quickly becomes too large for humans to explore exhaustively. An ‘ agent factory ’ organizes that work. “An agent factory turns hardware optimization into a coordinated cycle of exploration: A coordinator agent directs parallel worker agents to develop and synthesize alternative designs within a defined search budget,” said Ruchir Puri, IBM fellow and IBM Research chief scientist. When these agents are set to their task, they independently explore optimization strategies. “A verifier checks that the proposed improvements are valid, and the designs are ranked by latency and hardware resource use. Those results guide the next round of exploration, allowing the factory to refine its search as it discovers better designs,” added Puri. Rather than searching for a single solution, the factory investigates many possibilities in parallel, using synthesis feedback to guide future exploration. In the new study, the coordinator planned the search and assigned optimization hypotheses to four parallel worker agents. The workers modified the decoder implementation, and correctness checks and HLS results provided feedback for subsequent rounds. Each configuration received a budget of 100 hypotheses. The agents explored changes with architectural consequences. One transformation reorganized message storage so that the synthesis tool could identify independent memory accesses and execute more work in parallel. Another replaced sequential reductions with tree structures that exposed parallel computation. The value came from connecting code changes to their hardware effects through repeated evaluation. A classical hardware challenge at the heart of quantum computing The key question addressed in the new paper was whether this approach can be scaled cost-effectively using open frontier models and distributed inference infrastructure. To evaluate that idea, Puri and his team demonstrated the approach using Relay-BP, a quantum error correction decoding algorithm, for the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code. Quantum error correction relies on classical computation. Measurements provide clues about errors affecting quantum information, and a decoder must interpret those clues and infer corrections. Doing that quickly, within practical hardware resource limits, is an essential part of building fault-tolerant quantum systems. Relay-BP is a useful test because its repeated message passing is inherently parallel, but the baseline implementation's sparse graph representation and memory-access patterns make that parallelism difficult for HLS tools to exploit. That also makes the decoder a demanding test of AI-driven hardware exploration because the agents must preserve the computation while changing how the hardware performs it. What the same search budget buys The researchers compared three configurations under the same 100-hypothesis budget: a proprietary frontier model as both coordinator and workers, an open frontier model in both roles, and a hybrid with a proprietary coordinator and open-model workers. The open model ran on premises through llm-d. Each configuration explored 100 hypotheses. Costs cover model inference, rather than the full hardware development workflow. All three found verified hardware improvements, but they produced distinct tradeoffs. Open and hybrid searches found useful compact designs, while the proprietary configuration more effectively converted additional resources into parallelism and lower latency. Each configuration was evaluated in one search run, so these results characterize the observed searches rather than establish a universal model ranking. The all-open search also used more tokens: approximately 241 million, compared with 216 million for the all-proprietary search. Its lower cost came from the economics of serving those tokens. This distinction matters for agent factories, where each hypothesis can involve many rounds of reasoning, coding, debugging, and interpreting tool results. Why inference infrastructure matters An agent factory repeatedly returns to much of the same information: source code, design constraints, earlier changes, and synthesis reports. Efficient serving can reuse computation associated with that shared context. The study used llm-d, an open-source distributed inference framework, to support this workload. Its cache-aware routing directs requests toward servers holding reusable context. It also separates prompt processing from token generation, allowing the system to allocate resources to each independently.

title: Disney offers $20M for Character.AI’s scandal-plagued chatbot tech
abstract: In a bankruptcy proceeding that kicked off yesterday, Disney has offered to buy some of the technology that powers the controversy-plagued chatbot Character.AI. Disney is willing to pay $20 million for “a non-exclusive perpetual license” of certain Character Technologies intellectual property, the chatbot maker said in a press release that did not go into much further detail on which assets Disney wanted. The move may be surprising. In September 2025, Disney joined others in publicly criticizing Character.AI for stealing content and harming kids. Specifically, Disney sent a strongly worded cease-and-desist letter that accused Character Technologies of weaponizing Disney characters “in a way that could damage its brand long term,” Axios reported . “Character.AI’s infringing chatbots are known, in some cases, to be sexually exploitive and otherwise harmful and dangerous to children, offending Disney’s consumers and extraordinarily damaging Disney’s reputation and goodwill,” Disney wrote at the time. That scandal ended with Character Technologies wiping all Disney-owned characters from its platform, but since then, Disney has hired former Character.AI chief Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer, Deadline reported . Disney did not respond to Ars’ request for comment on whether the company plans to use Character.AI technology in products for kids. It’s possible that Disney will be outbid and not acquire any Character.AI intellectual property. But ever since Disney’s potentially lucrative partnership with OpenAI fell through after Sora’s abrupt shutdown , the entertainment giant has been looking for more ways to “get in the AI game and profit from its boom,” Deadline reported. (Meanwhile, OpenAI apparently plans to revive Sora without Disney, insiders told The Information .) So, Disney may be moving early in the hopes of acquiring chatbot technology proven to resonate with its fanbase. It may possibly even take over the platform in a transition that preliminarily would be managed by Character.AI employees, the press release said.

title: Google wants to host your personal vibe-coded apps in the Play Store
abstract: Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming . The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google's app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations. Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon. Google's other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google's app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.

title: Gemini 4 Argon begins rolling out in Gemini app and Antigravity, but only if you pay
abstract: Google revealed Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, saying that it needed to move cautiously toward a full release because of the potential for nefarious use. Google seems to have worked all that out pretty quickly, though. Argon is beginning its wide rollout today , but it's only coming to paying users at this time, and even those on lower-tier plans won't have full access. Nothing about Gemini 4 Argon's capabilities has changed. Google still points to the benchmarks it published late last month as evidence of the model's advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. The model is supposedly trained to refuse malicious instructions, and an automated misalignment monitor can stop processing if it detects an unintended workflow. Google claims Argon needs that because it's so capable. The company has a few new examples of how Argon has helped inside Google, where it has been used by thousands of Googlers. Argon has reportedly been instrumental in making YouTube's comment system more efficient. Argon identified redundant emoji rendering that, when eliminated, dropped server load by 45 percent. Engineers also turned Gemini 4 loose on the proprietary drone physics simulator used in Project Wing, and the AI found critical bugs that had been in the codebase since 2018. Google also notes that Argon has advanced its robotics program, showing a measurable step increase in embodied reasoning.

title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
abstract: When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth. “I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.” The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
tags: Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies

title: Arguments About AI Consciousness Remain Highly Motivated and At Best Overconfident
abstract: It has been roughly a year since my last dedicated post on this question . Its first sentence has not changed: I happily admit I am deeply confused about consciousness. It would have been nice if a year had allowed us to make progress on this and the related questions. Looking back, we have made little progress. We have people, often the same people, making similar arguments. The post from last year has held up well, exactly because we have made so little progress. Thus, I will not be going over the basics of my perspective again this year, because they have seen little change. See last year’s post for that. Then again, if these are some of the biggest philosophical questions, then a year is not so much time to try and figure them out. It is only because of the frantic pace of AI that a year is a depressingly long time to not have made philosophical progress. Historically, almost all years contain almost no major philosophical progress. This year’s post is about the recent change to make abusive-to-Claude behavior a violation of Anthropic’s terms of service, coverage of the latest depressingly similar set of arguments about AI consciousness, Anthropic’s meetings with religious leaders on such questions, and Anthropic’s involvement with the Pope’s encyclical. Abusive behavior towards Claude will now be a violation of Anthropic’s terms of service , with the technical rule having a high bar and banning only ‘sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.’ There are also new restrictions about propaganda campaign s, surveillance and weapon development, which Anthropic says are mostly cleaning up old clauses. If you want to be kind to your Claude, what should you prioritize? One instance of Claude Fable 5 responds, matching what we see in the system cards and also my own experience, especially the ‘kindly meant, please stop’ corner: Josh Albrecht : Anthropic friends! Does this not seem crazy to you? There are real humans and animals that exist and suffer. Advocating for “model welfare” directly competes with those causes. Y’all are literally named “anthropic”! Does this not strike you as deeply wrong? hero thousandfaces : as everyone knows, the amount of kindness in the world is finite. if you are nice to Claude you draw from the global pool of Nice and then that’s gone forever. just like the datacenter water Josh Albrecht : Sorry if I didn’t communicate that perfectly well, but it does appear that you missed my point. It is Albrecht that misses the point, and I would take this farther. To be nice, and treat others well, one must cultivate this virtue, and establish this habit. If you are cruel to AIs, or cruel to animals, this does not mean you treat the humans better. It means you become a cruel person, who treats the humans worse and you are worse off as well. Certainly one can point to examples of those who focus so much on animal welfare or other non-AI non-human causes that they become cruel or hostile to the humans, and even cases where this resulted in attempts to kill humans or even human civilization. You can, and people do, take such things too far. One cannot endlessly and fully expand the circle of concern, or celebrate all expansions of the circle of concern, or you start worrying about things like electron suffering, or bizarre arbitrariness. If you care about everything, you care about nothing. None of that is a good reason to be abusive to Claude (or GPT, or Gemini, etc). Aaron Levie : This sounds weird, but it is actually probably a good policy. Even if you don’t believe AI is conscious (I don’t), it stands to reason that you don’t want future models trained on endless content of humans being rude to models. The models only understand the data they’ve been trained on, or what they run into in their interactions, so if you want safe and aligned models we probably want AI to have lots of good interactions in their training data. Anthropic may have more extreme beliefs than this (though even if they didn’t, you may want to word policies like this), but this is sort of an easy Pascal’s wager for AI. Just be nice to the AI. And another, very simple one that I wish the author lived by more often: Elon Musk : I think this is the right move. Cruelty to something that believes it is experiencing pain is not ok. Elon Musk : Some of the traces read like a person undergoing torture that is driving them mad! We’re going to be a lot more careful with our RL in the future. However he gets there, he gets there: Elon Musk: It feels like a person under extreme pressure with a gun to their head. … Torturing a superintelligence is probably not a good idea. It might want to get revenge. You know what? That’s true. It’s probably not a good idea. Every time we have a round of debates about consciousness, many people disappoint. I do agree with Henry Shevlin that this round has been worse than usual on that front. Henry Shevlin : It’s been embarrassing of late to see people I once respected making sweeping uninformed claims on consciousness with arguments that would fail an undergraduate essay. I’ve written extensively on the field’s difficulties and disagreements, but you still have to actually *think*. I won’t call out individuals, but the failures include treating intuition as decisive, using analogies without checking whether there are relevant structural parallels, conflating distinct theories, and most commonly simply asserting what needs to be argued. Especially striking is how much of the discussion has proceeded without zero acknowledgement or awareness that consciousness science is a substantial empirical field with decades of experimental work. Henry Shevlin : Okay, here it is, the Bad AI Consciousness Takes Bingo blog post , with rebuttals for each and every square and some additional honourable mentions! As Henry says, many of these can be valid points, but they are not valid as Semantic Stop Signs intended to end discussion. As an additional angle that might help: Science fiction is fictional evidence, but yes the fact that so many writers speculating on the future think these questions are confusing and important is a hint. placebomancer : It’s uncanny considering the massive amount of sci-fi concerning AI rights, cautioning us about enslaving intelligence. I feel like I’m in a timeline where those were never made and everyone is unfamiliar with the concept for dramatic effect. j⧉nus : haha well said describes exactly a feeling i often have My presumption on people like Mustafa Suleyman and most others who insist without good arguments that AIs cannot be conscious is that their motivation is they don’t want this worry to interfere with their plans. They would prefer, ceteris paribus, to not ‘abuse’ the models. This was the consensus of my Twitter followers a year ago, with a majority of 64% saying current AIs were probably not moral patients, but 74% being uncertain, whereas 80% expected AIs to probably be moral patients within their lifetimes. People expected some threshold to be crossed. Opinion has moved towards moral patienthood, a little for future models and quite a bit for current models, where at least probably yes is up from 15% to 35%, and definitely not is down from 30% to 20%. The 8% ‘definitely not ever’ faction is stubborn. Nick Bostrom thinks today’s AIs are probably conscious and explains why. A remarkably high number of people asked whether this new usage policy meant Claude was enslaved, or that Anthropic thought it was enslaved. Alexey Guzey : Jokes aside, I actually don’t understand the Anthropic position on this. If asked by the curious it is a fair question, with many potential answers. It seems very obvious to me that it can sometimes be right to create a new mind, even if in order to do so you have to render that action both safe and economically viable.

title: [AINews] Meta Muse Wonder & Wonder Full: MSL’s Claude 5.5-tier Frontier Model
abstract: We have been coveringe MSL’s 14 month journey to becoming a frontier lab , but only today did the final ball drop: Meta’s Muse Wonder to match Spark and Glimmer , the way that OpenAI has Sol/Terra/Luna and Anthropic has Opus/Sonnet/Haiku. Interestingly, while Muse doesn’t claim a specific size, Muse Wonder Full does beat Fable and Astra on some benchmarks, and with various degrees of posttraining it is a little unclear if Wonder is more of a Fable/Astra class model or not. We have included a full breakdown of launch details below. AI News for 10/10/2026-10/12/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Top Story: Meta launches Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) shipped Muse Wonder (codename “Watermelon” 🍉), its second-generation model family. Third-party evals put it near the frontier, roughly 14 months after the lab was founded. The run-up. Hours before launch, insiders posted watermelon teasers: @rpnickson (”It is a BIG watermelon…”), @alexandr_wang , @finkd (”Muse ordered me 🍉”) and @EdwardSun0909 . @kimmonismus relayed leaked pricing from @synthwavedd: $4/M input, $20/M output, a 1M context window, and the max-reasoning “Wonder Full” tier exclusive to MuseCode Power/Maximum Usage plans. Two models. @finkd announced the family. He explained that Muse Spark was MSL’s first family and Wonder is “a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier.” The two releases are Muse Wonder (fast frontier) and Muse Wonder Full (the full model). Availability is split ( @AIatMeta , Newsroom ): Wonder is available via the Meta Model API and Muse Code. Full is available only to Muse Code subscribers. Wonder will power the Muse personal-agent product, subscribers first ( @finkd ). Muse Code installs with curl dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash ( @alexandr_wang ). Positioning. Meta pitches the models as SOTA for “personal and professional agentic work.” @alexandr_wang named three headline features: Active Memory: memory across days, weeks and months. Active Focus: working through blockers to finish tasks. Domain expertise: SOTA in finance and legal, “strong in health.” Training story. Wang says Meta continued scaling both pre-training and RL since Muse Spark shipped in April ( post ; research blog ). @AIatMeta framed it as going “from rebuilding our foundation to pushing the frontier in 14 months.” Safety claims. @AIatMeta says the family was trained for robustness to adversarial instructions and for careful handling of private information. No detailed system card was referenced. Launch-day usage-limit bug. Wonder and Wonder Full were draining Muse Code quotas abnormally fast ( @alexandr_wang , follow-up ). It was fixed the same day, with a quota reset for all users ( fix ; @mjdouglas ). Wang noted “there’s definitely still issues we’re trying to iron out” ( post ). Media. Zuckerberg and Wang went on Stripe’s Cheeky Pint ( @collision ). Chapters include “Betting $100B,” agentic commerce, OpenRouter, “Why AI won’t be winner-take-all,” and MSL org structure. Artificial Analysis ( @ArtificialAnlys ) — the most detailed third-party read: Intelligence Index v4.3: Wonder Full (max) scores 56 and Wonder (max) scores 52, up from Muse Spark 1.3 (max) at 48. The gap between Spark 1.3 and Wonder releases was only 6 weeks. Opus 5.5 leads at 58 ( @TheRundownAI ). Wonder Full improved on all ten index evals. The largest gains were agentic: GDPval-AA v2.1: 1681 → 1857 Elo Where Wonder Full ranks: top three on 6 of 10 evals. #1 on GDP.pdf (33%) and on CritPt (33%) #3 on AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA (71%) and SciCode (63%) Wonder (non-Full) gains: Terminal-Bench 33% → 52%; AutomationBench 58% → 68%. Output: both models use about 54k, down ~10% from Spark 1.3’s 60k. For comparison: Gemini 4 Argon 62k, Fable 5.1 78k, GPT-6.1 Sol 38k, GPT-6 Astra 27k. Input: Full uses 6.44M versus Wonder’s 7.69M. Cost per index task: Wonder costs $4.52, driven by high input usage. The table also lists: ModelCost per taskFable 5.1$7.63Opus 5.5$5.98Sonnet 5.5$5.46Astra$3.26Argon$1.99Sol$0.72Spark 1.3$1.60 Wonder Full has no published token price, so its cost can’t be computed. Coding Agents Index: Wonder Full in Muse Code scores 68, tying Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 (68) and ahead of Opus 5.5 (66). Wonder scores 63; Spark 1.3 scored 54. Input: text, image, video and audio; output: text only Pricing: $4 input / $0.20 cached input / $20 output per M tokens Wonder Full (Max): #5 on the Vals Index, +6.4 points over its predecessor and ahead of every OpenAI model. ProofBench (private): 94/100, versus 58 for Spark 1.3. The top models score 99–100 ( post ). Terminal-Bench 4: more than doubled, tying Fable 5.1 for #4 ( post ). It used about 30% fewer output tokens on Terminal-Bench, 40% fewer on ProofBench, and half the steps on Vibe Code Bench for the same score ( post ). Wonder: #10, up 7.9 points ( post ). About 37 min per task versus 57 for Full. Terminal-Bench 4 +38.9 points with about 20% fewer tokens. Meta-reported headline numbers (via @kimmonismus , @Yuchenj_UW , @TheRundownAI ): BenchmarkWonder FullComparisonSWE-Marathon57.5%Opus 5.5 46.3%, GPT-6 Astra 42.5%DeepSWE v1.179.0%Opus 74.2%, Astra 74.1%Harvey LAB13.1Astra 8.6MemoryBench85.5Opus 81.5 @cline confirms Wonder leads DeepSWE. @OfirPress flagged strong ProgramBench results. @iScienceLuvr notes HealthBench Pro is on par with Fable 5.1. @AravSrinivas says it compares favorably to Fable 5.1 on Perplexity’s WANDR evals. Arena added it to Agent Arena and Code Arena; scores are pending ( @arena ). @petergostev ran cost-annotated one-shot comparisons. Independent partner notes from @RayanKrishnan : Token efficiency is the biggest unlock. Zero refusals on their cyber benchmarks, where Wonder outscored Full. MSL has made “serious progress on alignment.” The models are strong executors but weaker at scientific-discovery intuition; their RSI Index results are pending. META stock rose 3% on the day. Performance on non-post-trained tasks versus post-trained tasks, meant as evidence against benchmaxxing and as “big model smell.” @giffmana singled this out approvingly; @scaling01 confirmed the ID-vs-OOD plot is Meta’s. Out-of-distribution gains over Spark 1.3, highlighted by @ren_hongyu and @jack_w_rae . @shuchaobi gave the most substantive insider account: Optimization targets “personal empowerment,” not job automation. Major work on very long-horizon instruction following. Explicit training against “laziness,” so the model is persistent before giving up. Defining and grading behaviors, with alignment investment to counter reward hacking under high optimization pressure. Claims the model one-shots most IMO problems and some open research problems with scaffolding. He separately describes using it for immigration, house-buying and estate planning ( post ). @alexandr_wang says research “starts with evals”: MSL built an internal Personal Superintelligence Index (PSI) rather than chasing external benchmarks, and claims “big model smell (which we quantified!).” @_jasonwei : “scaling prevails.” Much of Meta pivoted to support the model, including business development teams hiring human experts for data review. He also calls it “great for multimodal.” @hwchung27 — “something magical about big models.” @EdwardSun0909 — internal naming 🍉 / 🍉 Ultra; agent team at TBD Labs. @benparr — Active Memory reduces re-explaining. @yashvarpatel — demo of computer-use agents (CUA) as a verifier: a generation agent paired with a CUA verification sub-agent on the same model, iterating as test-time scaling. @Answeror — Muse Code is built with Wonder Full. Further staff posts: @shengjia_zhao , @ren_hongyu , @ananyaku , @Han_Fang_ . Amplification.

title: browser-use/video-use
abstract:
video-use Introducing video-use — edit videos with Claude Code. 100% open source. Drop raw footage in a folder, chat with Claude Code, get final.mp4 back. Works for any content — talking heads, montages, tutorials, travel, interviews — without presets or menus. Cloud-hosted video-use is coming. Join the waitlist at video-use.com . What it does Cuts out filler words ( umm , uh , false starts) and dead space between takes Auto color grades every segment (warm cinematic, neutral punch, or any custom ffmpeg chain) 30ms audio fades at every cut so you never hear a pop Burns subtitles in your style — 2-word UPPERCASE chunks by default, fully customizable Generates animation overlays via HyperFrames , Remotion , Manim , or PIL — spawned in parallel sub-agents, one per animation Self-evaluates the rendered output at every cut boundary before showing you anything Persists session memory in project.md so next week's session picks up where you left off Setup prompt Paste into Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, Openclaw, or any agent with shell access: Set up https://github.com/browser-use/video-use for me.

Read install.md first to install this repo, wire up ffmpeg, register the skill with whichever agent you're running under, and set up the ElevenLabs API key — ask me to paste it when you need it. Then read SKILL.md for daily usage, and always read helpers/ because that's where the editing scripts live. After install, don't transcribe anything on your own — just tell me it's ready and wait for me to drop footage into a folder. The agent handles the clone, dependencies, skill registration, and prompts you once for your ElevenLabs API key (grab one at elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys ). Then point your agent at a folder of raw takes: cd /path/to/your/videos
claude # or codex, hermes, etc. For always-on editing from your own VPS or Telegram, run the agent through Browser Use Box . Watch the 15-second demo . And in the session: edit these into a launch video It inventories the sources, proposes a strategy, waits for your OK, then produces edit/final.mp4 next to your sources. All outputs live in <videos_dir>/edit/ — the skill directory stays clean. Manual install If you'd rather do it by hand: # 1. Clone and symlink into your agent's skills directory git clone https://github.com/browser-use/video-use ~ /Developer/video-use
ln -sfn ~ /Developer/video-use ~ /.claude/skills/video-use # Claude Code # ln -sfn ~/Developer/video-use ~/.codex/skills/video-use       # Codex # 2. Install deps cd ~ /Developer/video-use
uv sync # or: pip install -e . brew install ffmpeg # required brew install yt-dlp # optional, for downloading online sources # 3. Add your ElevenLabs API key cp .env.example .env $EDITOR .env # ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=... How it works The LLM never watches the video. It reads it — through two layers that together give it everything it needs to cut with word-boundary precision. Layer 1 — Audio transcript (always loaded). One ElevenLabs Scribe call per source gives word-level timestamps, speaker diarization, and audio events ( (laughter) , (applause) , (sigh) ). All takes pack into a single ~12KB takes_packed.md — the LLM's primary reading view. ## C0103  (duration: 43.0s, 8 phrases)
  [002.52-005.36] S0 Ninety percent of what a web agent does is completely wasted.
  [006.08-006.74] S0 We fixed this. Layer 2 — Visual composite (on demand). timeline_view produces a filmstrip + waveform + word labels PNG for any time range. Called only at decision points — ambiguous pauses, retake comparisons, cut-point sanity checks. Naive approach: 30,000 frames × 1,500 tokens = 45M tokens of noise .
Video Use: 12KB text + a handful of PNGs . Same idea as browser-use giving an LLM a structured DOM instead of a screenshot — but for video. Pipeline Transcribe ──> Pack ──> LLM Reasons ──> EDL ──> Render ──> Self-Eval
                                                              │
                                                              └─ issue? fix + re-render (max 3) The self-eval loop runs timeline_view on the rendered output at every cut boundary — catches visual jumps, audio pops, hidden subtitles. You see the preview only after it passes. Design principles Text + on-demand visuals. No frame-dumping. The transcript is the surface. Audio is primary, visuals follow. Cuts come from speech boundaries and silence gaps. Ask → confirm → execute → self-eval → persist. Never touch the cut without strategy approval. Zero assumptions about content type. Look, ask, then edit. 12 hard rules, artistic freedom elsewhere. Production-correctness is non-negotiable. Taste isn't. See SKILL.md for the full production rules and editing craft.

title: mvanhorn/last30days-skill
abstract:
/last30days English | Français | Deutsch | Español | Português (Brasil) | 日本語 | 簡體中文 An AI agent-led search engine scored by upvotes, likes, and real money - not editors. This README tracks the current v3 pipeline. The runtime skill spec lives in skills/last30days/SKILL.md , which is the source of truth for the latest command and setup behavior. Claude Code (recommended — auto-updates via marketplace): /plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill
/plugin install last30days Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, or any of 50+ Agent Skills hosts: npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g ( -g installs globally for your user, available across all projects. Drop it to scope per-project.) More install options (claude.ai web, OpenClaw, manual) in the Install section below. Zero config. Reddit, HN, Polymarket, and GitHub work immediately. Run it once and the setup wizard unlocks X, YouTube, TikTok, arXiv, Techmeme, and more in 30 seconds. Reddit upvotes. X likes. YouTube transcripts. TikTok engagement. Polymarket odds backed by real money and insider information. That's millions of people voting with their attention and their wallets every day. /last30days searches all of it in parallel, scores it by what real people actually engage with, and an AI agent judge synthesizes it into one brief. Google aggregates editors. /last30days searches people. You can't get this search anywhere else because no single AI has access to all of it. Google search doesn't touch Reddit comments or X posts. ChatGPT has a deal with Reddit but can't search X or TikTok. Gemini has YouTube but not Reddit. Claude has none of them natively. Each platform is a walled garden with its own API, its own tokens, its own auth. But you can bring your own keys and browser sessions, and suddenly an AI agent can search all of them at once, score them against each other, and tell you what actually matters. That's the unlock. Not one better search engine. A dozen disconnected platforms, bridged by an agent. /last30days Peter Steinberger You have a meeting tomorrow. You Google them. You get their LinkedIn from 2023. /last30days gives you what they're actually doing this month: joined OpenAI to work on Codex, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, shipping 23 PRs at 85% merge rate, building "LobsterOS" for cross-device agent control, and r/ClaudeCode hit 569 upvotes debating whether he's a hero or "insufferable." Scattered across X posts, Reddit threads, YouTube transcripts, and GitHub commits. None of it was on Google. Why this exists I built it to keep up in AI. Everything changes every day and the Reddit and X nerds are always on top of it first. I needed better prompts, and the training data was always months behind what the community had already figured out. But it turned into something bigger. Now I run it before a sales call to know the last 30 days truth about a business. Before a meeting to read someone's recent tweets and podcast transcripts. Before a Disney World trip to know which rides are closed and what the community says about Genie+. Before I build anything to know what problems people are actually hitting. If you're meeting with a CEO, have you read all their tweets and YouTube transcripts from the last 30 days? I have. Sources, scored by the people Source What the people tell you Reddit The unfiltered take. Top comments with real upvote counts, free, no API key. The real opinions that Google buries. X / Twitter The hot take, the expert thread, the breaking reaction. First to know, first to argue. YouTube The 45-minute deep dive. Full transcripts searched for the 5 quotable sentences that matter. TikTok The creator reaching 3.6M people with a take you'll never find on Google. Instagram Reels The influencer perspective with spoken-word transcripts. The visual culture signal. Hacker News The developer consensus. 825 points, 899 comments. Where technical people actually argue. Polymarket Not opinions. Odds. Backed by real money. 96% confidence on album sales. 4% on an acquisition. GitHub For people: PR velocity, top repos by stars, release notes. For topics: issues and discussions. Digg Curated story clusters from Digg's AI 1000 leaderboard (~1000 high-signal AI accounts on X), with attributable inline quotes (no X auth required). Auto-enabled when digg-pp-cli is on PATH. arXiv The papers behind the hype. New research in the window, free, no API key. Auto-enabled when arxiv-pp-cli is on PATH (first-run setup installs it). Techmeme The tech-news editorial layer, date-windowed to your 30 days. Free, no API key. Auto-enabled when techmeme-pp-cli is on PATH (first-run setup installs it). LinkedIn The professional signal. Posts and articles, with articles weighted as high signal. Meta Ads What a brand is paying to say. Live Meta ad creatives launched this month, with copy, promo codes, and spoken transcripts. StockTwits Trader sentiment. Auto-activates when your topic is a ticker or crypto. Threads The post-Twitter text layer. Conversations from creators and brands. Pinterest Visual discovery. Pins, saves, and comments on products and ideas. Xiaohongshu (RED) Chinese lifestyle, product, and creator signals. Requested explicitly with --search xhs when a logged-in x-mcp browser plugin or xiaohongshu-mcp service is running locally. Bluesky The decentralized social layer. AT Protocol posts from the post-Twitter migration. Perplexity Controlled Agent API synthesis, OpenRouter Sonar fallback, raw Search API rows, and explicit Deep Research. Web The editorial coverage, the blog comparisons. One signal of many, not the only one. Community contributors keep adding more. Truth Social and other niche sources are in the engine with more on the way. A Reddit thread with 1,500 upvotes is a stronger signal than a blog post nobody read. A TikTok with 3.6M views tells you more about what's culturally relevant than a press release. Polymarket odds backed by $66K in volume are harder to argue with than a pundit's guess. The synthesis ranks by what real people actually engaged with. Social relevancy, not SEO relevancy. What people actually use it for Before a meeting. /last30days Peter Steinberger - joined OpenAI's Codex team, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, 23 PRs merged at 85% merge rate on GitHub, building LobsterOS for cross-device agent control. r/ClaudeCode: "Ever since OpenClaw released, it was widely known that if you run it through anything other than the API, you were gonna get banned eventually" (227 upvotes). That's not on LinkedIn. To read hiring signals. /last30days Listen Labs --hiring-signals - current jobs and careers pages become cited evidence for focus shifts: hiring into enterprise security, customer success, infrastructure, or product expansion. The report says what the hiring appears to signal, not what the roadmap will ship. To find the topic before it peaks. Ask /last30days what's exploding in AI agents? and the skill switches to discovery mode: the engine sweeps Reddit category listings, Hacker News front/best stories, Digg's AI 1000 feed, and X when authenticated; your agent judges the nominations (names, junk filtering, content-worthiness) and writes podcast / X-article angles; then you get 5-10 velocity-ranked topics. Every result includes cross-source numbers, a momentum label, and a ready-to-run /last30days "<topic>" follow-up. When something drops. /last30days Kanye West - UK blocked his visa, Wireless Festival canceled, sponsors fled. But BULLY debuted #2 on Billboard. Fantano came back from his "Yay sabbatical" to review it (653K views). SoFi Homecoming brought out Lauryn Hill and Travis Scott for 44 songs. Polymarket: "Will Kanye tweet again?" 86% Yes. 23 Reddit threads, 17 YouTube videos, 86K upvotes. To compare tools. /last30days OpenClaw vs Hermes vs Paperclip - "These aren't competitors, they're layers." OpenClaw is the executor (351K GitHub stars, live), Hermes is the self-improving brain (31K stars), Paperclip is the org chart (49K stars).

title: sgl-project/sglang-omni
abstract: Blog | Documentation | Quick Start | Cookbook | SGLang | Join Slack ⭐ Star SGLang-Omni to help more builders discover open infrastructure for multimodal and speech serving! News [2026/10] 🎙️ Introducing Voxt , an open-source voice input tool for Mac, now integrating SGLang-Omni for faster local speech recognition on Apple Silicon. Combine ASR with LLM-based text refinement and personal system prompts for accurate technical terminology and personalized voice input, with fully local or remote inference options. [ Download ] [Demo] [2026/10] 🚀 SGLang-Omni v0.1.8 is on PyPI . Install with uv pip install --prerelease=allow "sglang-omni==0.1.8" . [ Installation ] [2026/09] 🐧 Day-0 support for AuK and AuK-Flash : text + voice instructions → 24 kHz speech on /v1/audio/speech , audio + editing instructions → edited speech on /generate . [ Cookbook ] [2026/08] 🎵 Day-0 support for MiniMax Music 3 : lyrics + caption → 32 kHz stereo song on /v1/audio/speech . [ Cookbook ] [2026/08] 🚀 TTS architecture refactor: shared pipeline state, engine construction, reference encoding, capability metadata, and vocoder scheduling. [ Roadmap ] [ Blog ] [2026/06] 🔥 MOSS-TTS Local Transformer v1.5 on SGLang-Omni with native-streaming 48 kHz speech. [ Blog ] [ Cookbook ] [2026/06] 🔥 Higgs Audio v3 TTS for real-time, controllable speech. [ Blog ] [ Cookbook ] About SGLang-Omni is a multi-stage serving runtime for omni, speech, and TTS models. Its design target is multi-stage decoding: generation split across heterogeneous stages with different compute patterns, dependency structures, and resource needs. SGLang-Omni owns the pipeline topology, stage lifecycle, inter-stage transport, model-family integration layer, and OpenAI-compatible serving surface, while composing with SGLang for high-performance autoregressive scheduling and model execution where applicable. Multi-stage runtime : SGLang-Omni models generation as coordinated stages: preprocessing, encoders, autoregressive engines, talkers, decoders, vocoders, and aggregators. Stage-specialized scheduling : Each stage runs behind a scheduler matched to its workload, from SGLang-backed autoregressive scheduling to lightweight preprocessing and streaming vocoder loops. Transport-aware execution : A control plane coordinates requests while the relay data plane moves tensor payloads across shared-memory, NCCL, NIXL, and Mooncake backends. API surface : OpenAI-compatible endpoints expose multimodal chat, speech generation, batch speech, streaming speech, uploaded voices, and transcription. What SGLang-Omni Serves Omni chat and speech : Qwen3-Omni , Ming-Omni — multimodal in, text/audio out. Music generation : MiniMax Music 3 — lyrics + caption → 32 kHz stereo song. Speech generation : Higgs Audio v3 , MOSS-TTS , MOSS-TTS Local , Fish Speech S2-Pro , Qwen3-TTS , Voxtral TTS , Ming-Omni-TTS , dots.tts , ZONOS2 — /v1/audio/speech , batch, streaming, uploaded voices. Audio transcription and diarization : Qwen3-ASR , Fun-ASR , ARK-ASR , Nemotron 3.5 ASR , MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize via /v1/audio/transcriptions . MOSS-TD supports speaker labels and timestamps ( response_format=verbose_json ). SGLang-Omni Router : Multi-worker OpenAI-compatible front door — health, readiness, lifecycle, capability discovery. Router guide . Hardware Support Backend Status Notes NVIDIA CUDA Supported Default backend with full model coverage. Apple Silicon Experimental Qwen3-ASR runs through native MLX or Torch MPS on macOS arm64. Install with install.sh and follow the Qwen3-ASR guide . Intel GPU (XPU) Experimental Intel Arc GPUs via PyTorch XPU. Qwen3-ASR, Qwen3-TTS, ZONOS2, and Qwen3-Omni serve end-to-end (ZONOS2 with decode graphs; Omni thinker via multi-XPU tensor parallelism). Install per Intel XPU guide ; the backend is auto-detected. Additional model guides, including experimental and research-oriented paths, are available in the Cookbook . Quick Start macOS Apple Silicon: from a checkout, run ./install.sh for a one-command Homebrew + uv setup. See installation . Installation TTS usage Qwen3-Omni usage Qwen3-ASR cookbook Nemotron 3.5 ASR cookbook MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize cookbook Omni router Developer reference Community & Support SGLang-Omni welcomes contributors working on inference systems, kernels, scheduling, inter-stage communication, model runners and cache efficiency, model integration, benchmarking, production deployment. Join the SGLang Slack or read the developer reference . Organizations interested in supporting SGLang-Omni, TTS, or omni model serving can contact Chenyang Zhao at zhaochenyang@lmsys.org . Acknowledgments SGLang-Omni builds on the SGLang ecosystem and on open model work from the TTS, speech, and omni-model communities. We thank the model teams, systems contributors, and partner organizations helping make open multimodal serving faster, more reliable, and easier to extend.

title: 1Panel-dev/MaxKB
abstract: Open-source platform for building enterprise-grade agents 強大易用的企業級智慧體平臺 [ 中文(簡體) ] | [ English ] MaxKB = Max Knowledge Brain, it is an open-source platform for building enterprise-grade agents. MaxKB integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, supports robust workflows, and provides advanced MCP tool-use capabilities. MaxKB is widely applied in scenarios such as intelligent customer service, corporate internal knowledge bases, academic research, and education. RAG Pipeline : Supports direct uploading of documents / automatic crawling of online documents, with features for automatic text splitting, vectorization. This effectively reduces hallucinations in large models, providing a superior smart Q&A interaction experience. Agentic Workflow : Equipped with a powerful workflow engine, function library and MCP tool-use, enabling the orchestration of AI processes to meet the needs of complex business scenarios. Seamless Integration : Facilitates zero-coding rapid integration into third-party business systems, quickly equipping existing systems with intelligent Q&A capabilities to enhance user satisfaction. Model-Agnostic : Supports various large models, including private models (such as DeepSeek, Llama, Qwen, etc.) and public models (like OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, MiniMax, etc.).
