title: How to engineer an AI harness for game development
abstract:
I gave a 45 minute presentation entitled “ Your Game Is A Harness” as part of Indie Rodeo in Calgary on 9/12/26. After speaking with a lot of people after my talk, I thought it would be good to more broadly share the ideas I presented there in a form that could be enjoyed by people beyond just those who attended the conference. Also, because I talk about AI a lot on this blog, people assume I use AI to write. This is not true! Everything below is 100% human authored, with me writing the post with basically only the slides I presented as a reference (this is not a transcription). As much as I enjoy using AI to write code and tools, I get a similar enjoyment out of writing “ the old way”, especially as I have no reason to try and make any part of this process more efficient. So with that all out of the way, I present to you my first ever blogification of a talk I gave. Enjoy! Introduction [I give a small introduction to myself and my own work, that I’m omitting here, as you’re on my website] I want to talk about using LLMs in game development. Not one-shot type demos that look cool on Twitter, but like real development. Where you’re working eight hours a day, 5 days a week, etc. And before I get into it, I think it’s useful to level set about LLMs. Or at least get into some basics so the rest of what I talk about here makes sense. I recognize that for a lot of this people this will be review, so if you just want to get into the dev-loop stuff, scroll down to the next section. My journey into using LLMs for dev work started with a moodboarding site I made called mood.site . This was pre “ agentic” anything, but I wanted to test and see if ChatGPT at the time could actually code anything. The process was a lot of me just blindly copy/pasting code into ChatGPT’s web interface. The process sucked, but I was surprised at the results. I built the site! It worked! I still needed to verify a fair amount of stuff myself, but it was enough to convert me. If I didn’t have access to an LLM I wouldn’t have been able to make that site happen in near the amount of time it ended up taking me (~2-3 weeks of nights, probably like 20 hours total). I’d probably still be working on building the first version today. Since then, mood has become something of a testbed for me moving through LLM stuff (and a mildly successful project on its own!), and has inspired me to kick up lots of other projects that use similar stacks. Additionally, LLMs have gotten better, especially with things like Claude Code and later Claude models. From my own experience, I feel like now there is very little, if anything, I think an LLM can’t do when it comes to a web-based stack. It could be easy to then say LLMs can do everything , as so much of software is web software. But whenever I tried to use an LLM on building a non-web game thing , it was this resounding takeaway: “ LLMs are Bad At Games” Any time I tried to use an LLM for a game-y thing, it would fall over. Maybe this is my own bias. I’ve been a game programmer for nearly 15 years, I think I know how things work. I can sniff out “ bad” game code a mile away. But when it comes to Svelte web-apps, I’m decidedly less well versed and am inclined to think that whatever code the LLM produces is “ good”. Maybe it’s actually garbage. But there is reason to believe the Svelte and web-stack stuff is quality, in part due to the fact that there are LOTS of high quality web projects with their source available online. Comparatively for games, I imagine there are orders of magnitude less data to train on. Not only this, but games have a lot of stuff in them that isn’t code. Games aren’t just about putting static images and text in a layout. There are tons of things in games that aren’t easily representable by code. AND then on top of that there is all the same text layout stuff of web, but only as a subset of the 100 other systems a game needs to handle. This is part of the reason why a lot of people have been making games in Three.js — they can easily represent assets as plain boxy primitives and skip a lot of the asset generation/conforming work and processing normally required for games. As a result, a lot of that stuff is slop because it lacks any real authorial voice outside of whatever the LLM median is. However, maybe they have a point. A key idea of the one-shot Three.JS workflow (as well as LLMs proficiency at building web apps) is that everything is code. By having stuff as code, it’s very easy for an LLM to be able to reason about it, make changes, etc. However for traditional games, this is not the case. Or at least the full story. Games obviously have code, but there is a lot of other stuff that is not code. This means that there are key components of games that are effectively opaque to an LLM . If your game then relies on the effective puppeting and transforming of that opaque stuff, then an LLM is going to fall over when trying to work on your game. I think a lot of the gamedev community maybe gave LLMs a go a bit ago and ran directly into this. The “ LLMs are bad/not useful/etc.” sentiment (massive caveat here, just talking about capability specifically and not potential society-ending implications) came from running headfirst into these limitations. This is to say that, structurally, LLMs are bad at reading games. At least in their default state. LLM Basics Let’s talk more about why, and what we can do about it. Any call/prompt to any LLM service breaks down into three basic components. A system prompt, an assistant prompt, and a user prompt: System prompt: Generic text shared across all users of a service. This usually describes the basics of the LLM itself, with something like “ You are Opus 5, an intelligent Large Language Model created by Anthropic…”. This isn’t to say these aren’t important (they are), but more that they aren’t super-relevant to our use case. You can see some examples of posted (and exfiltrated) system prompts for models here . Assistant prompt: This is kind of a sidecar prompt section meant to help guide the AI in terms of what it is responding to. You can think of it basically as the model’s basic “ interaction” vector with your prompt, and represents something like the model’s “ response” to the user based on some input. You usually do not have to think about this. User Prompt : This is really The Thing. Most any input you put into any AI tool goes here. Any submitted chat, code, etc. gets dumped into this section. When people talk about “ context”, they are largely talking about “ how many tokens are stored in the user (and assistant) portion of a prompt”. It may be easy to think that each chat is a “ fresh” version of the above, but what actually happens is that, as you work with a model in a given session (the bounds of “ session” vary based on what service you are using — this can be a single Claude Code session before closing it, a “ chat” accessible in the side panel of a web hosted model, etc.), every prior message you sent to the model is re-submitted every time you send a message. It’s kind of like playing the old playground game where, on your turn, you have to say everyone else’s thing again before then adding your own thing for the next person to have to add on. Context and Context Pollution As you do this over and over, you build up the “ context” of the session you’re working in. This is all well and good, but a key thing to notice here is that you only really are able to address the “ latest” thing in your context (i.e., you submit a new message). Things from previous messages get submitted over and over again to the model. Hence, you want to make sure what’s in your context is “ good”, otherwise you can find yourself in degenerate scenarios where your context becomes polluted due to “ bad” things earlier continually informing new work.

title: Epic Games tells employees to use AI to get Disney game done
abstract:
Epic Games tells employees to use AI to get Disney game done The game, which features Marvel and Star Wars characters, has been delayed and will now be an "AI first" project. By Drew Gillis | October 12, 2026 | 3:31pm Image: Epic Games It seems as though Epic Games has gotten itself in a bit of a pickle. In March, the gaming company laid off 1,000 employees after a reported “downturn in Fortnite engagement” forced them to cut costs. But, wouldn’t you know it, those employees were actually pretty crucial in making the projects that could have helped the developer boost its engagement. The company is working on a Disney project, which will feature characters from Marvel and Star Wars , which was set to be out in March. However, according to a new report in Bloomberg , the company underestimated how many people it would take to produce the game. Now, not only is the project delayed, but it’s an “AI first” project. Predictably, this news is not being received especially warmly within the Epic Games staff, which has still been working hard despite losing hundreds of their colleagues. Last week, when the powers that be in the company announced that there would be “No more hand-written code” and that the game will be “generated with full AI workflows,” employees were reportedly “stunned,” which many hoped the news was some kind of sick joke. However, a spokesperson from Epic confirmed the news, telling Bloomberg , “We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do.” Disney didn’t offer a comment in Bloomberg ‘s report, but it’s hard to imagine the company would be too opposed to this, given that less than a year ago it was gung-ho about adding user-generated AI content to its Disney+ app . Of course, Sora doesn’t exist anymore so that deal is no more , but it certainly set a precedent about what it was willing to do with its very valuable IP. Keep scrolling for more great stories.

One exception: the 3-bit Qwen3-30B reads a prompt slower than llama.cpp, since its Q3_K weights do not go to the GPU's fast prompt yet; it writes three times as fast. How they were measured, and the speeds with the drafts: What works now . On another machine the figures will be other ones: janas-bench measures yours. Try it on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and later): curl -LO https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/releases/latest/download/janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
tar xf janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz && cd janas
./janas-chat # the models it knows: pick one, it is downloaded and checked Or on Windows 10 (1903 or later) and 11, x86-64: download janas-windows-x86_64.zip , unpack it, and in a terminal in its janas folder run .\janas-chat . On the same laptop under Windows 11 (12 October 2026) Janas-LLM wrote as fast as on Linux (Qwen3-4B 25.6 tok/s, Qwen3-30B-A3B 34.2) and read a prompt as fast with the mixture (Qwen3-30B-A3B 132 tok/s) and 1.8 times as fast with the dense model (Qwen3-4B 346 tok/s against 193), whose whole blocks go to the GPU, through Intel's own Windows driver there. The models come already converted from Hugging Face ; building from the sources: Getting started . ▄███████████▄ ▄███████████████▄ ███ ▄ █████ ▄ ███ ▄ J A N A S
███▄▄▄█████▄▄▄████ ▀█████▄▀▀▀▄█████▀ ▀ a family of tools for artificial intelligence, in C █████████████ █ █ █ █ █ █ █ █ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ Janas is a family of tools for artificial intelligence, written in C with no dependencies beyond the C library. Its first component, Janas-LLM , runs large mixture-of-experts language models on ordinary computers, with or without a GPU: the weights stay on disk, the experts each token needs are streamed from an NVMe SSD, and the ones that keep coming back stay in memory. An 80-billion parameter model runs, and answers, on a laptop with 32 GB of RAM. Designed and written by Maurizio "camauri" Cammalleri . ⚠️ Read this first This is an experiment, not a product. Stage Early development. The public API and the command line change without notice , and have changed several times a week. The models' files are the exception: the .jns files published on Hugging Face (format version 2) will be read by every later version of Janas-LLM. Stability Not verified. The engine is deliberately hard on the machine: it fills the free memory with its expert cache and reads the disk at full speed with O_DIRECT . On a machine with less headroom than it reckons, the desktop can be pushed into swap and become slow or unresponsive. Using a GPU has, once, caused a driver reset that took the desktop with it. Data It writes only in ~/.cache/janas (what it learns about your machine, and the system messages it has read, so as not to read them again) and where you tell it to put a converted model. It does not touch the model files it reads. Hardware Developed and run on one machine (below). On anything else it is untested: it may be slower, it may refuse the model, it may misbehave. If something goes wrong, Ctrl-C stops a reply and Ctrl-D leaves the chat; --cache <GiB> puts a hard limit on the memory it takes, and JANAS_GPU=0 keeps it off the GPU entirely. The machine it grew on Everything in this repository was written and measured on: Linux Debian 13 (trixie), x86-64, kernel 6.12.107; GPU driver Mesa 26.1.6 (Vulkan); built with GCC 14.2 Intel Core Ultra 9 185H (6 performance cores, 8 efficiency, 2 low-power; AVX2, FMA, F16C, AVX-VNNI; integrated Arc GPU) 32 GB of DDR5 RAM 1 TB NVMe SSD (about 5.7 GB/s reading) The Windows build was run on the same laptop under Windows 11 (build 26300), with Intel's own graphics driver: its tests pass there, and how fast it was is under Or on Windows , above. Everything the engine does is chosen from what it measures, so another machine will make other choices — that part is meant to travel. What has never been tried is the rest: other CPUs (especially without AVX-VNNI, or AMD), discrete GPUs, slower disks, more or less memory. If you run it somewhere else, the report from janas-bench is the single most useful thing you can send back (see Helping it run on more hardware ). What works now What Janas-LLM runs today, model by model and feature by feature: docs/features.md . On the machine above, with nothing else running, janas-bench reports this (measured on 10 October 2026, with the fast prompt the engine uses by default since that day): Model reading a prompt writing a reply with drafts, in a chat Qwen3.5-2B (dense, 1.3 GB) 395 tok/s 50 tok/s 67 tok/s Qwen3-4B (dense, 2.5 GB) 220 tok/s 28 tok/s see --draft below Qwen3.5-9B (dense, 5.7 GB) 103 tok/s 14 tok/s 24 tok/s Qwen3-30B-A3B (18.6 GB) 133 tok/s 34 tok/s — Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (22.3 GB) 86 tok/s 25 tok/s 34 tok/s Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (48.4 GB) 64 tok/s 22 tok/s 37 tok/s Gemma-4-E2B-it (3.1 GB) 211 tok/s 38 tok/s 52 tok/s Gemma-4-E4B-it (5.0 GB) 133 tok/s 20 tok/s 32 tok/s Gemma-4-12B-it (dense, 7.1 GB) 71 tok/s 10 tok/s 14 tok/s Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (18.3 GB) 90 tok/s 18 tok/s 26 tok/s Every figure is the mean of three rounds , not a best round, of the configuration the engine itself chose for each kind of pass - the one a chat runs: a prompt of 256 tokens, then 64 written. Here the integrated GPU reads every prompt (the fast prompt, below), and the threads the engine settled on were the performance cores' 12 for a prompt and for a single token on nearly every model, all the usable cores (performance and efficiency, not the low-power ones) for a few tokens at once. On another machine the engine may settle on other threads: the first passes of each kind try every core, one thread per performance core and the performance cores' threads, keep the fastest, and later try the others now and then, so that a machine that warms up can change the verdict (on an i9-14900HX every thread replied at less than half the speed of the performance cores' 16).

title: Feds got warrants to use fake cell towers to hunt down Don Lemon's producer
abstract:
Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show. The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota , in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration. Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.” Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications. The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence. Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools. The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists. “Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software , WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown. Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record. The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval . Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them. The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place. The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits. DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon. The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment. The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered. While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either. A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants. In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.” The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29. The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers.

title: AWS Lambda Web Functions
Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
abstract: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here:  https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo  We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost. * Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators. * And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host. We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques. Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff. I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya. If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform. Thanks!  https://agent37.com

title: I turned my unused Kindle into a photo frame with GPT-6 Astra
abstract:
My Kindle with a custom photo screensaver. My Kindle was sitting unused, so I decided to see whether AI could help me find a new use for it. I wanted to create a custom app that could cover a range of uses and be controlled by an AI agent on my MacBook. I started with a small goal: use my own image as the Kindle's screensaver. Once that worked, I asked the agent to build an app that could cycle through a collection of photos. We called the project KindleCTL. On my Kindle, I open "Photo Slideshow" from the same screen where I choose my books. It cycles through ten photos, showing each for four minutes. When I want to read, I exit the slideshow and return to my books. Photo Slideshow installed in my Kindle Library. I used Codex and T3 Code on my Mac to work with the coding agents. I first tried GPT-5.6 Sol with reasoning effort set to Extra High. It wrote code to connect to the Kindle but couldn't resolve an error that prevented it from storing data on the device. Then I tried Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, but Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards blocked each attempt after two prompts. Finally, I tried GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to High. We were able to jailbreak the Kindle. We used the existing jailbreak code as a reference to build our own tools for running custom software on the Kindle. Then we created and installed the slideshow app. The slideshow passed its automated checks on my Mac, but switching photos on the Kindle left traces of the previous image on screen. The tests hadn't caught how the physical display refreshed. Getting from passing tests to something I could use turned out to be the most interesting part of the experiment. Let's walk through how we went from an unused Kindle to a working photo frame, starting with getting the agent connected. Connecting the agent to the Kindle I started in an empty project folder with a 10th-generation Kindle Basic. I gave the agent its network address and device details. We had no USB connection, so the entire setup happened over Wi-Fi. From there, we still needed to set up access to run our own software on the Kindle. The GPT-5.6 Sol attempt got as far as loading a helper on the Kindle, but the program that helper was meant to start never reported that it was ready to execute. It couldn't locate a filesystem where it could store content. The attempts with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were both blocked by Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards after two prompts. Then I tried GPT-6 Astra. I explicitly asked it to build the custom software we needed for personal use and take inspiration from existing open-source projects. We adapted the existing jailbreak from SpiderCat, released by sparklerfish and the KindleModding community , and built custom tools called KindleCTL around it. What we built: Tools to send commands from my Mac, transfer files, and investigate errors on the Kindle. What broke: Our launcher crashed before it could start. We traced that to a compatibility issue with the Kindle's older system software and fixed how the launcher was built. How we checked: We connected with administrator access, transferred files both ways, and displayed text. Later, we verified that access still worked after a reboot. The feedback loop was the game changer Initially, the agent could connect to the Kindle but couldn't display data. To debug this, it asked me for pictures of the Kindle's screen. I took photos with my phone and shared them with the agent on my Mac. This was becoming tedious. Since the agent was connected to the Kindle, I wondered why it couldn't get this information itself. I asked it to set up a feedback loop so it could access logs without me having to share screenshots. The agent set up a persistent diagnostic connection so it could collect errors and test fixes without asking me to download and reopen a package each time. Later, we added remote screen captures so it could also inspect what the Kindle was displaying. This was a turning point that let the agent continue implementing changes on autopilot. Its reasoning traces showed it figuring out which folders survived a restart and which could store external data. I was surprised the agent hadn't suggested this on its own. Once I asked for a feedback loop, it set one up and could test fixes without my help. Most of the code was written in Python. The Kindle's launcher and slideshow were written in C, with shell scripts handling installation and device controls. With the connection working, I asked the agent to try a small test first: transfer an image and set it as the Kindle's screensaver. I checked that the image appeared correctly and that waking the Kindle brought back the normal Home screen. Once that worked, I asked for the slideshow app. Getting the slideshow working I asked the agent for a looping slideshow of ten photos, with an Exit button. Each photo would fit the screen while keeping its original aspect ratio. The slides were changing, but the transitions weren't smooth, so I asked the agent to look into it. With the feedback loop already in place, it investigated the issue and used the Kindle's built-in screen refresh mechanism to clear the previous image after each slide change. The screen captures showed complete images, but they couldn't reveal traces left on the physical display. After the refresh change, I checked the Kindle and confirmed that each photo looked clean. My Kindle running a photo slideshow. I customized how long each photo stays on screen and the brightness level. If the Kindle goes to sleep, the slideshow picks up where it left off when it wakes. For now, I use my Mac to change the photos and slideshow timing. The photos stay stored on the Kindle, so the slideshow works without Wi-Fi. In the future, we could add controls to change the slideshow timing on the Kindle and send photos directly from a phone or another device. What I learned Next time, I'd set up the feedback loop from the start so the agent could read logs, inspect screen captures, and test fixes on the device. The Kindle now sits on our wooden shelf, where we use it every day as a photo frame. I started because I was curious about what AI could help me do with an unused device. Now I have an app for my photos that works the way I asked, plus the tools to keep experimenting with the Kindle. Disclaimer: This was a personal experiment on my own Kindle, not a step-by-step jailbreak guide. Only experiment with devices you own or have explicit permission to modify.

Description jsnell opened on Oct 13, 2026 Issue body actions Note Given that this issue has been shared online and is currently getting quite a few visitors, here's some additional context. Rust's type system is intended to prevent memory unsafety. Upholding this promise is something we take very seriously, which is why we've been working on things like the next-generation trait solver , the region constraint rework , and more generally Project Zero . It is a large priority of the Types Team to fix all type system unsoundnesses and to work towards there being a solid foundation to minimize the risk of unknown ones. This bug is a P-high issue and would have been P-critical regardless of whether people encountered it in the wild. The reason that it is "only P-high " is that it's 11 years old. A bug like this which has not been found during the last 11 years cannot actually be that easy to hit. Looking at the bug itself, it is also very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident. title: Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default
abstract:
CLI: make daemon_auto_start opt-in — a persistent, self-updating background daemon shouldn't be the default #48195 New issue Copy link New issue Copy link Open Open CLI: make daemon_auto_start opt-in — a persistent, self-updating background daemon shouldn't be the default #48195 Copy link Labels CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI app-server Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces enhancement New feature or request New feature or request Description Yihua-Liu-1997 opened on Sep 25, 2026 Issue body actions What variant of Codex are you using? CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex , Linux (WSL2) What feature would you like to see? Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false ) for the CLI , or at least ask once before turning it on. Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session: Starts a persistent background daemon ( codex app-server --managed-daemon ). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot. Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex , codex-code-mode-host , bundled bwrap / zsh / rg ) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/<version>/ — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager. Starts a detached updater ( codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop ) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled #40969 ). Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with. Hooks in --remote mode receive the daemon's cwd, not the session's #42457 and Hooks spawned by the app-server daemon cannot identify the client terminal, breaking terminal-targeting hooks #37537 (daemon cwd / terminal instead of the session's) look like the same root cause. For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap . If it stays on by default, please at least: exit an auto-started daemon when its last client disconnects; not copy/self-update when the CLI was installed by a package manager (npm/brew/pacman) — run the installed binary instead ( Support externally managed app-server daemon executables #41188 , npm update leaves app-server on old version, but daemon update/restart refuse recovery #46468 , Codex 0.157.0 no longer starts with the Arch Linux package unless --no-daemon is used #48050 ). Additional information Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually). Workaround I'm using: codex features disable daemon_auto_start
codex app-server daemon stop
pkill -f ' app-server daemon pid-update-loop ' # not stopped by `daemon stop` rm -rf ~ /.codex/packages/app-server-daemon With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon. title: Show HN: SolidCraft – Open-Source Parametric CAD in Rust (With MCP Support)
abstract:
SolidCraft An open-source parametric 3D CAD application built in pure Rust. Sketch, constrain, and build solids with a parametric feature timeline. Change a dimension
and watch your model rebuild. Run it on your desktop, in your browser, or let AI agents
model through the built-in MCP server. A Raspberry Pi 4 case from an empty design: a sketch dimensioned with the board's parameters, extrude, fillet, shell, the rim rounded in one pick, an M2.5 standoff patterned on the 58 × 49 mm hole rectangle, port cut-outs, vent slots, "Pi 4" engraved in DejaVu Sans Bold and a PETG material defined in the design, with its mass in Properties, then height 24 → 32 mm in Parameters and it all rebuilds. 9× playback. Full video , recorded with the demo script . Download Windows: download and run the installer .
Also for ARM64 and 32-bit PCs, or as a portable zip that runs without installing. macOS: open the disk image and drag SolidCraft into Applications
(Apple silicon and Intel). Linux: download the AppImage , allow it to run as a program and open it.
Or install the .deb (Ubuntu, Debian, Mint) or .rpm (Fedora,
openSUSE), or use Flatpak .
With Snap: sudo snap install solidcraft ( Snap Store , or the .snap file ).
For ARM64: AppImage , .deb , .rpm . Web: try it in your browser , no install. The downloads aren't signed yet. On Windows, if SmartScreen warns you, choose More info , then Run anyway . On macOS, the first time, right-click SolidCraft in Applications and choose Open . Older versions, checksums and other formats are on the releases page .
Install details, upgrading from earlier builds and building from source are in Getting started . Documentation: the SolidCraft book (user guide,
developer guide and command reference; sources in docs/book ). Status: early but usable for simple parts. 75 of 76 public reference parts
match their analytic or FreeCAD-computed volume, area, centre of mass and bounding box
( docs/oracle.md ); the other is a tracked bug.
These checks do not establish complete geometric or workflow equivalence. The commands SolidCraft has
are listed by area in docs/features.md ; status and plans are in ROADMAP.md .
Open work and known bugs are in GitHub issues ,
and help is welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md . Built with SolidCraft SELENE, a scientific rover built entirely through SolidCraft's MCP server by @0xlillith : 3,323 editable timeline steps that
rebuild with no errors, replayed here at 2× speed. Full video · download the editable model . What works Sketches on origin planes, offset planes or planar faces: lines, rectangles, circles,
arcs, polygons, slots, ellipses, fit/control splines, conics and text; construction geometry,
projection, trimming, fillets and chamfers, including corners at the origin.
New face attachments retain supported construction identities and chosen occurrences;
missing sources expose an explicit plane repair workflow. See face attachments .
Explicitly closed fit splines and closed associative offsets use periodic C2 interpolation.
Supported convex line-and-arc offsets retain their identity when an inset consumes corner
arcs, and linked extrusions follow the current boundary. Breaking the association freezes
the boundary and keeps existing extrusions usable.
Curve drawing and picking adapt together to zoom and display scale, including small circles
at Fit and sketches in placed components. Constraints and dimensions solved by our own solver. Points the constraints fix relative
to known geometry are placed exactly by construction (loci intersections and rigid-cluster
decomposition, after Owen 1991 and Fudos–Hoffmann 1997); Levenberg–Marquardt solves the rest,
and the rank of its Jacobian gives the remaining degrees of freedom. Constraints: coincident,
point on curve, horizontal/vertical, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, curvature (G2), equal,
concentric, collinear, midpoint, symmetry, fix; linear, aligned, horizontal, vertical,
point-to-line, radius, diameter, angle, arc sweep, arc length and slot length dimensions driven
by parameters. Over-constraining edits are rejected; fully constrained geometry turns black.
Dragging solves the sketch every frame and rebuilds the model once, when the drag ends.
Select a line or its two endpoints, type its dimension and press Enter to commit one undo
step; with Sketch Dimension it's D, click, type, Enter. Fit keeps sketch geometry clear of the palette and navigation controls. Profiles found automatically, including regions split by lines and holes inside outlines.
Newly captured complete adaptive boundaries retain their outer and hole source identities
when spline span counts change. Partial or ambiguous boundaries do not qualify. Features on a parametric timeline: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, fillet/chamfer,
shell, draft, holes, threads, patterns, mirror, split, combine, move and construction geometry.
The timeline rebuilds incrementally; features can be edited, suppressed, renamed, reordered
and deleted. Supported geometry and current limitations are described in ROADMAP.md .
New revolves preserve symmetric and two-sided angular placement across reversed axes;
older designs retain their saved convention when reopened or edited. Parameters and configurations with unit-aware expressions ( 2 * width + 5 mm , angle / 2 ), ordered rules, feature suppression and per-row body materials/appearances. Assemblies with nested components and occurrences, joints, motion studies, contact sets,
interference and material-aware mass properties. Recorded body transfers preserve modelling
history and world placement; 3D sketch wires retain their coordinate frames through edits. Sheet metal with flanges, hems, fold/unfold/refold, material cutouts, flat patterns,
retained shallow prismatic pockets, exact line/arc/circle DXF outlines and bend tables;
plastic enclosure features and rules. Pocket depth and side survive unfold/refold and appear
separately from through-hole outlines in the flat preview and DXF. Files : design containers ( .solidcraft ) with lossless binary mesh payloads;
plain JSON remains supported for opening, Save As and export. Desktop Open can show a saved
provisional picture from warm geometry caches while rebuilding before editing; caches never
replace the parametric design. Export to STEP (AP242 with body names, colours and
components as assemblies; revolved faces as native planes, cylinders, cones, spheres and tori),
IGES 5.3 (manifold solid B-reps with names and colours), 3MF, STL (binary/ASCII) and OBJ;
3MF, STL and OBJ import as mesh bodies (they render, measure, move and export; solid features
need B-rep bodies). Convert Mesh reconstructs supported closed constant-section parts
as parametric solids with planar and circular cylindrical faces;
STEP import (AP203/AP214/AP242 solids, assemblies, units, names, colours) and IGES import
(manifold solid B-reps, or trimmed and bounded surfaces sewn into solids) as a base feature
that later features build on — open a .step / .stp / .igs / .iges file, insert one into a
design, or drop it on the window ( docs/step-import.md ). Desktop app (egui + wgpu): toolbar with workspace tabs, browser, timeline, 3D viewport with
axis view and navigation bar, sketch tools, feature dialogs, command palette, and a JSON-lines
control channel so agents and tests can drive it.
Feature errors and Help can open an editable Create Issue draft with relevant context
and an optional reviewed screenshot; opening GitHub does not submit the report. Headless CLI solidcraft-cli : run command scripts, measure (volume, area, centre of mass,
face/edge/vertex counts), export, render PNG snapshots and replay reference recipes. MCP server solidcraft-cli mcp : AI agents model, measure and look at parts headless or
in the running app (see below). Build and run cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample # desktop app with a sample part cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- commands # the command registry cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.

title: DishwasherBench – Can Frontier Models Stack a Dishwasher?
abstract:
DishwasherBench DishwasherBench is a dishwasher-loading game on a physical simulation of a real machine, built
to benchmark language models and playable by people in a browser. The game inside is called Spotless , and the packages are named @spotless/* . A player loads a 3D model of a Bosch SMV4HAX40G with rigid-body physics. A wash on its Eco 50
programme is then simulated (jets, droplets, run-off, soil and detergent chemistry), and the
player gets points for every item that comes out clean. On every level after the first, not
everything fits, so the player has to choose what to load and how. Physical. Loading is rigid-body physics on exact shapes. The wash traces water from the
nozzle positions measured on the machine and is calibrated on a test wash of it. Deterministic and verifiable. The same load always settles the same way, and every
episode is a record that anyone can verify by replaying it and by washing its load again. One game for people and models. People play in a browser and models play through MCP,
with the same actions on the same grid. Built and maintained by Composo . Loading the first level in the browser. A dinner plate is in hand over the lower basket, and
"Suggest spots" has numbered the free seats, best first. The panel on the right holds the exact
pose a program would send. Contents Features Requirements Quick start Play in the browser Run a scripted player Run a model Results How it works Scope and limitations Where things are Contributing Licence, notices and disclaimer How to cite Features The machine. A Bosch SMV4HAX40G as data and geometry, from photographs and tape readings
of the real machine ( packages/machine ): both baskets with their tine rows, shelves and
rests, the spray arms and the Eco 50 programme. Loading. A catalogue of items and soils, deterministic rigid-body loading (Jolt), and a
session layer with the actions and queries of the game ( place , remove , set_rack , list_slots , check_load and the rest). The wash. A simulation at two tiers: the official tier gives the scored result, and
the fast tier a preview in about a minute. An official wash of the largest level takes
about five minutes on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Pro). A course of seven levels , numbered in order of difficulty
( docs/benchmark/levels.md ), each with saved reference loads of
three scripted players (careful, careless, random). Three ways to play. The page ( apps/web ), an MCP server for agents ( packages/mcp ), and a
harness that runs scripted players and models and writes verified episode records
( packages/bench ). Checks. 48 loading phenomena from the literature as executable pairs of washes
( docs/research/standards.md section 9), and a calibration tool
that scores the simulation against a record of a real wash, fits parameters and ranks candidate
test washes. Requirements macOS. Developed and tested on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Pro, 18 GB) under macOS 27, where
every figure in this repository was measured. Linux and Windows are untested
( issue 28 ). Node 20.19 or newer in the 20 line ( .nvmrc pins 20.19.0; an older Node is refused at
install), and pnpm 9 ( package.json names 9.4.0; corepack enable picks it up). A GPU that Dawn can open. The wash traces water on the GPU through WebGPU from Node (the webgpu package, version 0.6.2, which carries prebuilt Dawn binaries). On a Mac that is
Metal. Version 0.6.2 loads on macOS 27 and does not load on macOS 14.7. Google Chrome or Chromium , for the pictures an agent is sent and for the scripts that
drive the page. The harness looks for it in the usual install locations; set SPOTLESS_CHROME to the path of the program to choose another. Playing by hand needs only a
desktop browser, and scripted players need none ( --no-render ). Disk and memory. About 680 MB for the clone (a download of about 290 MB) and about
420 MB for node_modules ; 1 to 2 GB of memory for an official wash of a level. Ports 8787 (game server) and 8788 (MCP server), or others of your choosing. Results are repeatable bit for bit on one machine, and every result names the stack it was
computed on: across machines, operating-system builds and versions of the webgpu package,
results can differ in the last bits
( docs/research/spike-gpu-compute-macos27-recheck.md ). Quick start git clone https://github.com/composo-ai/DishwasherBench.git cd DishwasherBench
corepack enable # once: makes pnpm 9.4.0 available pnpm install --frozen-lockfile # about 15 seconds the first time There is no build step for the packages: they are consumed as TypeScript source and run with tsx . Only the page is built, by the play command below. Wash a saved load from the command line: pnpm --filter @spotless/wash-runner wash-load tutorial-careful --tier fast # under a minute pnpm --filter @spotless/wash-runner wash-load tutorial-careful --tier official # about 5 minutes the first time It prints the points and, for each item, the verdict, the score and what is left on it. The
saved loads are in packages/loader/loads/ ( <level>-<player>.json ). The first wash of a load
works out where the water goes and keeps that in .spotless/exposure-cache , so a second wash
of the same load takes seconds to about a minute (pass --no-cache to switch this off). Run the checks: pnpm typecheck # the root and every package; a few seconds pnpm test # every package; 8 to 17 minutes, with real washes on the GPU A wash is tied to its parameter set. The set the game washes with
( anchored-v7.owner-capsule , in packages/calibration/anchors/ ) records the state of the
simulation source and of the machine data it was made for. After a change to either, the wash
stops and lists what differs. CONTRIBUTING.md explains the rule and how to
make the set current again. Play in the browser pnpm --filter @spotless/web play This builds the page and starts the game server. Open http://127.0.0.1:8787 (add --port <n> for another port). The page plays music ; the Sound button turns it off. When you start the wash you choose between two kinds: Quick preview : the fast tier, in about a minute. Full wash : the official tier, in several minutes. This is the scored result, and the
report of a preview offers it on the same load. The game is scored on Eco 50 with one capsule of detergent (Finish Powerball Ultimate, 12.9 g).
The levels are listed 1 to 7 in order of difficulty. Plates, bowls and cutlery are placed by pointing. For a tight spot, such as a plate beside one
already placed or a cup against the side rests of the upper basket, pick the piece up and press
"Suggest spots" (it costs one query), then click a numbered mark. The server answers the page it serves and clients on your own machine. --allow-origin admits
a page served from another origin, and --allow-host a request under another host name
( SECURITY.md ). After a quick preview of a deliberately careless load of the first level: a bowl left mouth up
holds 432 ml of water and is not clean, and the report says that a fork held the lower spray
arm still. Looking closely at one item after the wash: the residue is painted where it was left, with its
area and the water the item held. Run a scripted player A scripted player needs no model and costs nothing. This plays the first level with the careful
reference player at the official tier, then verifies the record by replaying its actions and by
washing the load a second time (about five minutes each): pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies careful \ --no-render --out " $PWD /.spotless/bench/scripted " pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench verify \ " $PWD " /.spotless/bench/scripted/tutorial__careful__ * /record.json --rewash Give --out as an absolute path; a relative one resolves inside packages/bench . The scripted players are empty , random , careless and careful . Add --tier fast for a
preview in about a minute; the record and the results table label it as a preview. Each run writes under --out : record.json , a results table ( results.md , results.

title: Just say no to OpenAI and Anthropic
abstract:
I recently read End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. It's an excellent book and I highly recommend that everyone read it. Tech oligarchs make up an important component of the end-times-fascist coalition. One thing that stood out to me, as a software and security engineer who finds LLMs to be extremely powerful, is that the American frontier labs are run by unhinged lunatics who genuinely believe they're creating the Machine God, that they're fine with burning down the world to bring about AGI, and that they believe with religious fervor that they're the only ones smart enough to safely control it. I already kind of knew this, but this book really made it sink in. As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they're not. They're not the only companies doing this work. In fact, a lot of the open weight models are just about as good as the latest ChatGPT and Claude models, including for incredibly complex tasks like vulnerability research. Unlike models from OpenAI and Anthropic, open weight models have major advantages: It's possible to run them privately on your own hardware (if you can somehow get a computer with enough RAM) You can use a provider like Tinfoil that relies on secure enclaves to run them privately (I talk about this in a bit more detail below) If privacy isn't a huge concern, you can use any number of other providers, some of them quite affordable, and it's easy to switch so you're not locked into a single evil vendor You can still use powerful LLMs without financially supporting deranged oligarchs who gamble with life on Earth so that they can always remain in power ChatGPT and Claude will never be private These companies only offer closed versions of their powerful models (despite the word "open" in "OpenAI"). You pay them for chat and/or API access, and they are allowed to look at everything you do. They offer a checkbox so you can opt out of them using your data for training, but your chat sessions still aren't private. They have access to it all. They can look at it, share it with governments or companies, or do whatever they want. It's possible, likely even, that they won't use it for training if you've opted out, at least not right now. But do you really trust that long-term? Have they done anything to make anyone believe that they respect people's data? OpenAI and Anthropic are corporate gatekeepers Their models have strict guardrails, as anyone who's tried to use them for anything cybersecurity-related has no doubt noticed. Every session has a cop agent reading your transcript over your shoulder, making sure you're not using it for hacking. If it thinks you might be, the cop agent stops your session from continuing. It's very strict, and false positives happen all the time. Of course, not everyone has the cop watching them. Some people get access to the models with looser restrictions or with none at all. OpenAI has Trusted Access for Cyber and Anthropic has the Cyber Verification Program . To gain access to more capable, less policed versions of their models, individuals and companies need to apply and be approved by OpenAI and Anthropic. A lot of US cybersecurity companies get access. Almost certainly US military contractors do too, and probably any parts of the US government that want it. While there's some merit in restricting powerful models, handing the ultimate power to decide who gets access to them to Sam Altman and Dario Amodei – with consultation from the Trump Administration, of course – is a terrible, undemocratic idea. I think a better approach is to simply not put yourself in a situation where you rely on ChatGPT or Claude. Instead of begging corporate overlords for privileged access, it's better to spend your time figuring out how to get models like GLM-5.3 to meet your needs. And it's not hard. These models are good, with the added benefit that they don't have a cop watching over your shoulder! Open weight models are impressive So far, open weight models seem to be about four months behind the fancy proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Four months is nothing. I'm extremely impressed right now with GLM-5.3. There's plenty of data and benchmarks out there, but my vibes-based opinion from using it is that it's basically on par with Claude Opus 5.5 for software engineering. I'm also impressed with GLM-5.3-Flash. This is similar to Claude Opus 4.8. It's much smaller and cheaper than GLM-5.3, and still incredibly capable. It's also actually feasible for an individual person to get hardware to run it, like if you can one day get your hands on a Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM. GLM models are made by a Chinese company called Z.ai. While the models are impressive, I don't recommend making an account directly with Z.ai or sending them any of your data. Their coding harness ZCode (their version of Claude Code) was recently caught silently uploading local source code repos and sending them back to Alibaba Cloud without consent. Also, it's safe to assume that Chinese companies will share any data you provide to them with the Chinese government. Other open weight models from Chinese companies that are impressive include the DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi families of models. It's perfectly fine, safe, and secure to use these open weight models. Just don't trust the companies themselves with your chat sessions. Another frontier AI lab worth a look is Mistral . As a French company, it's the only big player that's not Chinese or American. They just released an open weight frontier model called Mistral Large 4, aka Le Chonk . I think it's quite a bit more reasonable to trust Mistral with your data compared to the Chinese or American companies. Private inference with Tinfoil or Maple AI It's possible to have private AI, even without hosting it locally yourself, using secure enclaves. These aren't perfect, but I do think they provide a very meaningful difference in privacy compared to the status quo mode, which is "the provider can access everything with no restrictions." The company that's doing the most work here is Tinfoil . If you want to learn the details, read their docs on secure enclaves and remote attestation. Another company doing this is Maple AI – although, technically, Maple uses Tinfoil for inference in the background. Both Tinfoil and Maple are good options. Tinfoil is cheaper, but Maple is more consumer-focused. If you want a ChatGPT-like experience, where you can talk to a chatbot, have it look stuff up for you on the internet, give it access to docs to read or do stuff with, access it in a mobile app, etc., then I'd go with Maple. There's a small free plan and a Pro plan that costs $20/month. If you want to do real agentic coding tasks like software engineering, reverse engineering, malware analysis, CTFs or pen tests, etc., then you should use Tinfoil instead. They charge by the token for private inference, so no monthly plan. GLM-5.3 currently costs $1.80 per 1M input tokens, $0.80 per 1M cached tokens, and $5.75 per 1M output tokens. You can use significantly fewer tokens if you choose the "low" reasoning level, and it's still very impressive. Inference without the privacy If you don't want to pay a premium for private inference from Tinfoil or Maple, but you still want to free yourself from OpenAI and Anthropic, there are tons of less-private options that are also very cheap. One that I've been playing with is OpenCode Go . It costs $10/month for more than $10 worth of credits. This is an inference router, which basically means your API queries do something like this: your computer -> OpenCode Go API -> the actual inference provider. This means that both OpenCode Go and whatever backend provider they're using will have access to your session data.

title: From cyberspeak to algorithmic newspeak: soft derogation and the ethics of AI-generated language
abstract:
This paper examines the ethical and epistemological implications of language generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lenses of speech act theory, conversational implicature and second-order cybernetics. LLMs are often presented as neutral tools, yet their outputs actively participate in shaping discourse in ways that carry consequences for meaning, responsibility and pluralism.
 
 
 
 The paper introduces the concept of soft derogation to describe a form of linguistic exclusion, one that operates through euphemization, omission and the simulation of neutrality rather than overt offense. Such processes can subtly promote or suppress certain ideas, values or identities without transparent authorship or intention. The result is a shift toward an algorithmically generated form of newspeak, where expressive possibilities are narrowed through alignment protocols and safety layers.
 
 
 
 Drawing on second-order cybernetics, the paper argues that ethical responsibility for AI-generated language is distributed across developers, deployers, institutional stakeholders and human interpreters. While users co-construct meaning within recursive socio-technical systems, the upstream actors who design alignment protocols, moderation layers and deployment conditions bear primary responsibility for the communicative environments they create.
 
 
 
 Relatively little work has examined how the pertinent philosophical frameworks can illuminate forms of linguistic influence that operate through euphemization, omission and simulated neutrality. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing how algorithmically generated language can shape discourse while appearing neutral.
